newsitem.title: USA: NYS Assembly wants $193 million for better housing.
newsitem.headline: NYS Assembly wants $193 million for better housing.

text.p: The New York State Assembly, which is embroiled in a crucial battle over rent controls with the Senate, on Tuesday proposed spending $193 million more to make housing more affordable and pay for structural repairs.

"In our largest cities and in smaller communities as well, too many of our citizens face an impossible choice between housing that is safe and housing that is affordable. This program will give them both as well as provide thousands of sorely needed, new construction jobs," said Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, in prepared remarks.

The Assembly's plan would develop or rehabilitiate over 25,000 housing units for the elderly or working families with excessive rent burdens or those who are living in units with leaking roofs, substandard heating, plumbing or electrical systems or other major, strucutural flaws, the Assembly said, in a prepared release.
More than 5,235 jobs would be created, and the state funds would be leveraged with more than $280 million of private sector funds, it added.

Part of the controversy over state regulations that set increase for rent-controlled and rent-stabilized apartments, most of which are in New York City, stems from landlords' concerns that they cannot afford to improve their buildings under the present system.

The New York State Senate Majority Leader, Joseph Bruno, who wants to shift to a free-market system, has threatened to let the rules expire on June 15, and the issue has become a crucial fight holding up progress in reaching a new state budget for fiscal 1998, which was due on April 1.

The Speaker, who along with his Senate counterpart and the governor, has been criticized for negotiating major items of legislation out of the public eye, among the three of them, vigorously attacked Bruno for not working to resolve the differences between the Senate and Assembly about a host of issues in a public forum or through a conference committee.

"What we have now is a stealth legislative body," he said, saying the only clear position he knew the Senate had taken was on its desire to cut sales taxes on charter buses. A spokesman for Bruno was not immediately available to comment.

"It's time to try a new way. The failed policies of the past may not work. Twelve years of three men in a room hasn't produced a timely budget," he told reporters at an Albany news conference. New York State now has missed its April 1 deadline for a budget for the 13th year in a row.
Silver also attacked the Republican governor for not setting forth his views on rent decontrol, and attempting to act as a behind-the-scene negotiatior.

Pataki, who also held a news conference in Albany, told reporters that there had been preliminary discussions, adding he felt the best way to resolve the issue was to try to bring the "various parties," whom he did not identify, to a consensus.

"The goal is to solve a problem, the goal is to reconcile very divergent positions and that requires having a concept as to where you want to go, but then being flexible in how you achieve that, and that's what we will look to do."

Silver, who cited a U.S. census bureau study that found 646,000 New Yorkers pay over half of their income in rent, predicted that a handful of Republican Senators, who represent districts with sizable numbers of voters who live in rent-regulated apartments, would be able to insert their views into a measure the Senate adopts.
The Senate Republicans on Modnay stifled an effort by the minority Democrats to bring a bill extending the rent rules to the floor.
Silver also forecast that failing to extend rent rules would cause New Yorkers, especially the elderly, to leave the state, not only for neighboring areas, but for Boston, for example.
